comparison.summary: Same subarray enumeration; your solution stops sooner once product exceeds the current GCD × LCM.
details: Both extend each starting index while maintaining the product, GCD, and LCM, and record a length when product equals GCD × LCM.
Your code stops at prod > g * l. The existing Python computes a global limit lcm(*nums) * max(nums) and stops only after the product exceeds that limit.
For positive input values, once product exceeds the current GCD × LCM, extending the subarray cannot restore equality. Your earlier stop is valid.

Your code writes out gcd and lcm helpers. The existing Python uses its math functions. Both have O(n²) worst-case time for the bounded values and O(1) extra space. No JavaScript or TypeScript implementation was saved.

solutions.title: Extend subarrays with product, GCD, and LCM
solutions.approach: Try each starting index i and extend the subarray with end index j, updating prod, its product; g, its GCD; and l, its LCM. Record its length whenever prod equals g * l. Stop extending that start once prod is greater, because adding more positive values cannot restore equality.
solutions.timeComplexity: O(n²) for the stated bounded values
solutions.intuition: Trying every subarray is manageable for these constraints if its product, greatest common divisor, and least common multiple are maintained as the right end moves. There is also a useful stopping rule: once the product exceeds GCD × LCM, further positive values cannot restore equality. The product multiplies by the new value, while GCD × LCM can grow by at most that same factor.
hints: Fix a left end and extend the right end. Which three running quantities avoid recomputing the whole subarray?
Use the Euclidean algorithm for GCD and LCM(a, b) = a / GCD(a, b) × b.
After adding a positive value, the GCD cannot increase and the LCM grows by at most that value. What does that imply once the product is already larger than GCD × LCM?

pseudocode.concept: Extend each subarray while updating its product, GCD, and LCM; stop when equality becomes impossible.
steps: Implement GCD using repeated remainders, then compute LCM from GCD.
Start the best length at zero.
For each start index i, reset prod to 1, g (GCD) to 0, and l (LCM) to 1.
Move end index j from i to the end, incorporating nums[j] into prod, g, and l.
If prod equals g * l, update the best length with j - i + 1.
If prod is greater than g * l, stop extending this start index.
Return the best length after every starting index has been considered.

solutions.explanation:
1. The Euclidean loop replaces the larger GCD problem with a remainder problem until the second argument is zero. LCM divides by the GCD before multiplying.
2. Starting with product 1, GCD 0, and LCM 1 makes the first extension work naturally: all three running quantities become the first value. Each later extension updates the quantities for exactly the current inclusive range.
3. Equality means this subarray qualifies. Its length is j - i + 1 because both endpoints are included.
4. For a new positive value v, the product becomes old product × v. The GCD cannot increase, and the new LCM is at most old LCM × v. Thus, once old product is greater than old GCD × old LCM, the inequality remains strict after another extension. Breaking is safe.
5. A product below the target does not justify stopping. The code keeps extending in that case and tries every other left endpoint independently.

timeComplexityBreakdown.variables: n is the number of input values. The stated values are integers from 1 through 10.

phases.label: Initialize the best answer and reset state for each left endpoint
Try at most n(n + 1) / 2 subarrays; each extension updates product, GCD, and LCM

simplifications: O(n²) for the stated bounded values
timeComplexityBreakdown.note: The LCM of values from 1 through 10 is at most 2520, and the running GCD is at most 10. Euclidean GCD calls therefore take bounded work independent of n. With unrestricted values, their numeric size would also affect the bound. Early stopping reduces visited subarrays but does not increase this worst-case upper bound.
